title: Listening in Kedara
hook: listen to one Kedara hymn at dusk

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Kedara, and your line was tender evening. Which compliment and which criticism did you set down before sleep? Day one thousand one hundred eleven.

Dusk is the hour when titles fade. The office badge comes off. The uniform goes on the hook. In the half-light, a manager and an intern walking home look about the same. The practice for today is to listen to one Kedara hymn at dusk, and there's a hymn in this raga made for that hour. It's by Ravidas, the Bhagat who closes the Kedara section, and it's about what's left of a person when the labels come off. Today, listening in Kedara.
screen: `DUSK: THE TITLES FADE.` → `THE BHAGAT WHO CLOSES KEDARA.` → `RAVIDAS.`

segments.voice: We met Ravidas earlier, singing in Gond. Tonight it's one hymn, heard slowly. Here it is in Kedara, given in plain English, not word for word. A person may perform all the prescribed rituals and come from a high family, but if there's no devotion to the Lord in the heart, and no love for talk of the Lord, that person stands no higher than the one their society looks down on. Then Ravidas turns to his own mind: wake up, careless mind. Look at Valmiki, the poet of the old story, and how high devotion lifted him from a birth others scorned. Listen to the order of the hymn. First a verdict on others, then a wake-up call to himself. Ravidas doesn't stand outside the problem pointing in. He includes his own careless mind. And then he gives an example, not an argument: Valmiki. One life, lifted. Ravidas takes the scale that ranked people by birth and ritual and sets devotion in its place. Rank by family: gone. Rank by ceremony: gone. What remains is the heart. That's why dusk is a fitting hour for him. In the half-light, the labels fade, and what's left of a person is what they love. The Gurus set this hymn in their book, beside their own. Listening at dusk, there's no need to judge anyone, including yourself. Just hear a voice that turns first to its own careless mind, and let the light go. That's today's line: dusk in kedara.
screen: `HIGH BIRTH, RITUALS, NO DEVOTION.` · `WAKE UP, CARELESS MIND.` · `LOOK AT VALMIKI.` · `WHAT'S LEFT IS WHAT YOU LOVE.` · then, large: `DUSK IN KEDARA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take off the titles. Sit, and let the eyes soften as if the light is going. Silently, name one label you carry: your job title, a role in your family, a word others use for you. Let it fade on the out-breath, the way colors fade at dusk. Then another. Don't judge any of them; just let them dim for now. When the labels have faded, notice what's still here: breath, a body, whatever you love. Rest there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly. If you don't, simply stay with the breath. Later, at dusk if you can, listen to Ravidas's hymn in Kedara with the words in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Listening in Kedara. Hearing Ravidas at dusk: high birth and ritual without devotion count for nothing; what's left is the heart. Today's word.
Your line: dusk in kedara. As the light goes tonight, step outside or to a window for a minute, and let the day's labels go with it. Day one thousand one hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Ravidas's hymns are sung in kirtan in their ragas like the Gurus' hymns, and his teaching that birth and caste count for nothing before God is honored in Sikh communities and by the Ravidassia community.

without devotion in the heart, rituals and high family count for nothing.

options: argues his family should be ranked higher.
replaces the whole scale with devotion.
fork.reveal: Ravidas sets devotion where birth and ritual stood, and points to Valmiki, lifted by devotion from a birth others scorned.

original.note: Ravidas: the Bhagat whose hymn closes the Kedara section of the Guru Granth Sahib.
